prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Smart-city demonstration roads Road lighting for smart-city demonstration roads has no special requirements and may refer to other road types. 126 4.1.7 Public Transport 1. Location of bus stops A. Bus stops shall generally be set in conjunction with rail transit stations, shopping malls, hospitals, schools, residential areas, and other buildings, close to pedestrian entrances and exits, so as to reduce the walking distance for passengers boarding buses. 2. Setting of bus bays A. Bus bays should be set on arterial roads; on secondary arterial roads, whether to set bus bays shall be determined according to bus traffic volume. B. When bus traffic volume is low, straight curbside stops may be adopted after demonstration. Where land is constrained, bus platforms in reconstruction, expansion, or major repair projects may be set in conjunction with existing conditions. 3. Other requirements for bus stop setting A. The location of bus bays shall not encroach on pedestrian and non-motorized traffic space, and shall not affect the safety and order of pedestrian and non-motorized traffic. B. To avoid conflicts between buses stopping and non-motorized vehicles, the road may be locally widened, with the non-motorized lane set on the outside of the bus platform (bus shelter, stop sign, etc.). Where conditions are limited, the bus platform may be set within the facility belt of the roadside belt, and measures to slow non-motorized vehicles shall be taken. Figure 4.1-17 Design drawing combining bus stops and non-motorized lanes C. For roads in old urban areas where space is severely constrained, when curbside bus stops have to occupy the non-motorized lane, a motor-vehicle/non-motor-vehicle separation barrier shall be set upstream and downstream of the stop, and a slowing/yielding zone shall be set on the non-motorized lane. 4. Bus shelter setting A. Bus shelters should adopt an integral stainless-steel frame structure and be equipped with bus stop seats, light boxes, display screens, intelligent monitoring, lighting, illumination enhancement, and other facilities. Lighting and illumination enhancement shall meet relevant requirements. 127 Figure 4.1-18 Example of bus shelter and bus seat 5. Metro feeder connections A. In conjunction with bus planning, reduce long-distance co-linear routes with the metro, and increase vertical bus feeder routes and “Z”-shaped bus feeder routes; in conjunction with metro traffic recovery design, adjust the locations of bus stops to meet the needs of feeder bus routes and transfer distance requirements. B. According to station functions and passenger flow conditions, appropriately arrange non-motorized vehicle parking spaces at each station, and implement unified and orderly parking management in areas with concentrated demand for non-motorized vehicle parking.

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. For large urban intersections and traffic roads of larger scale, adopt smaller curb radii and prudently set up... Set channelized facilities to shorten crossing distances at intersections; bicycle waiting areas may be provided in areas where conditions permit. For residential streets with heavy pedestrian flows, compact intersections or raised intersections may be adopted to reduce vehicle speeds. Public transit travel scenarios. Around urban bus stops, priority should be given to traffic transfer and the needs of special groups. Enrich the service functions of the stop area, strengthen integrated bus stop design, and coordinate the layout of shelters, trash bins, public toilets, and other facilities, while providing barrier-free ramps. Improve the convenience of bus transfers and use: bus stops should be located as close as possible to community entrances and metro entrances, with parking areas for non-motorized vehicles and shared bicycles; in areas where conditions permit, covered walkways may directly connect the stop with surrounding buildings. Rail transit travel scenarios. At rail transit entrances and exits, priority should be given to traffic gathering and dispersal functions, while coordinating the needs of special groups, and providing plaza space for gathering and dispersal, a clear wayfinding signage system, small resting spaces, and a complete barrier-free facility system. Concentrated parking areas for non-motorized vehicles, public bicycles, and shared bicycles shall be set up, and emergency evacuation routes shall be clearly marked. In areas where conditions permit, corner plazas and pocket parks may be added; it is encouraged to integrate breakfast stalls, convenience stores, and other convenience service facilities with station entrances and exits, and to provide covered walkways between rail transit stations and surrounding public buildings. Smart-city demonstration roads Road lighting for smart-city demonstration roads has no special requirements and may refer to other road types. 126 4.1.7 Public Transport 1. Location of bus stops A. Bus stops shall generally be set in conjunction with rail transit stations, shopping malls, hospitals, schools, residential areas, and other buildings, close to pedestrian entrances and exits, so as to reduce the walking distance for passengers boarding buses. 2. Setting of bus bays A. Bus bays should be set on arterial roads; on secondary arterial roads, whether to set bus bays shall be determined according to bus traffic volume. B. When bus traffic volume is low, straight curbside stops may be adopted after demonstration. Where land is constrained, bus platforms in reconstruction, expansion, or major repair projects may be set in conjunction with existing conditions. 3. Other requirements for bus stop setting A. The location of bus bays shall not encroach on pedestrian and non-motorized traffic space, and shall not affect the safety and order of pedestrian and non-motorized traffic. B. To avoid conflicts between buses stopping and non-motorized vehicles, the road may be locally widened, with the non-motorized lane set on the outside of the bus platform (bus shelter, stop sign, etc.). Where conditions are limited, the bus platform may be set within the facility belt of the roadside belt, and measures to slow non-motorized vehicles shall be taken. Figure 4.1-17 Design drawing combining bus stops and non-motorized lanes C. For roads in old urban areas where space is severely constrained, when curbside bus stops have to occupy the non-motorized lane, a motor-vehicle/non-motor-vehicle separation barrier shall be set upstream and downstream of the stop, and a slowing/yielding zone shall be set on the non-motorized lane. 4. Bus shelter setting A. Bus shelters should adopt an integral stainless-steel frame structure and be equipped with bus stop seats, light boxes, display screens, intelligent monitoring, lighting, illumination enhancement, and other facilities. Lighting and illumination enhancement shall meet relevant requirements. 127 Figure 4.1-18 Example of bus shelter and bus seat 5. Metro feeder connections A. In conjunction with bus planning, reduce long-distance co-linear routes with the metro, and increase vertical bus feeder routes and “Z”-shaped bus feeder routes; in conjunction with metro traffic recovery design, adjust the locations of bus stops to meet the needs of feeder bus routes and transfer distance requirements. B. According to station functions and passenger flow conditions, appropriately arrange non-motorized vehicle parking spaces at each station, and implement unified and orderly parking management in areas with concentrated demand for non-motorized vehicle parking.

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant.
